passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel antihypertensive agent, Hypertensol, on systolic blood pressure (SBP) in adults with stage‑1 hypertension. A randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled trial enrolled 120 participants who were assigned to one of three groups: (1) Hypertensol 50 mg daily, (2) Hypertensol 100 mg daily, or (3) placebo. After 12 weeks of treatment, mean SBP and standard deviation (SD) were recorded. The study aimed to evaluate dose‑response relationships and compare the drug’s efficacy to placebo. The investigators also collected data on adverse events and medication adherence. The results are summarized in Table 1 below. The authors concluded that Hypertensol produced a dose‑dependent reduction in SBP, with the 100 mg dose achieving a mean reduction of 24 mm Hg compared to placebo.
stem: Which of the following statements best describes the data presented in Table 1?

options.A: The 50 mg dose lowered SBP more than the 100 mg dose.
options.B: The placebo group had the lowest mean SBP.
options.C: The 100 mg dose produced the greatest reduction in SBP compared to placebo.
options.D: All groups had identical standard deviations.

explanation: The 100 mg group’s mean SBP (126 mm Hg) is 24 mm Hg lower than placebo (150 mm Hg), indicating the greatest reduction. The 50 mg group is 12 mm Hg lower than placebo, so the 100 mg dose shows a dose‑response effect.
trap: Reversing the dose comparison and thinking the 50 mg dose lowered SBP more, when its mean (138 mm Hg) is 12 mm Hg higher than the 100 mg group's (126 mm Hg).

stem: Participants in this trial were randomly assigned to the three groups. What is the main purpose of random assignment?

options.A: To ensure every participant knows which dose they receive.
options.B: To make the standard deviations of all groups identical.
options.C: To distribute known and unknown confounding variables across groups by chance.
options.D: To remove the need for a placebo group.

explanation: Correct: Random assignment balances both measured and unmeasured participant characteristics across groups on average, so differences in outcome can be attributed to treatment. Why the others are wrong: A) participants being aware of their dose is the opposite of blinding and is not the purpose of randomization. B) randomization does not force equal variability; the SDs here are 10, 9 and 11. D) randomization does not replace a placebo; the placebo group supplies the comparison baseline.
trap: Confusing randomization (which balances confounders) with blinding (which prevents expectation bias).

stem: Assuming the standard deviations are equal, calculate the approximate 95 % confidence interval for the mean difference between the 100 mg and placebo groups.
explanation: Mean difference = 126 - 150 = -24 mmHg. With equal SD of about 10 and n = 40 per group, SE of the difference = sqrt(10²/40 + 10²/40) = 2.24 mmHg. 95% CI = -24 ± 1.96 x 2.24 = -24 ± 4.4, i.e. about (-28, -20) mmHg.
trap: Centering the interval on the 50 mg-versus-placebo difference (−12 mm Hg) or the 100 mg-versus-50 mg difference instead of the observed 100 mg-versus-placebo difference of −24 mm Hg (margin about ±4.4).

stem: Which of the following is NOT supported by the passage and Table 1?

options.A: Mean SBP in the 100 mg group was 24 mm Hg lower than in the placebo group.
options.B: Mean SBP in the 100 mg group was 12 mm Hg lower than in the 50 mg group.
options.C: Hypertensol was shown to reduce the rate of heart attacks and strokes.
options.D: Participants were randomly assigned and the trial was double‑blind.

explanation: Correct: The trial measured only blood pressure after 12 weeks; no cardiovascular events are reported. Why the others are wrong: A) 150 - 126 = 24 mm Hg, as stated in the table and passage. B) 138 - 126 = 12 mm Hg, from the table. D) the passage describes a randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled trial.
trap: Assuming a lower blood pressure automatically means proven fewer cardiovascular events.

stem: Which conclusion is best supported by Table 1?

options.A: Mean SBP was 12 mm Hg lower than placebo at 50 mg and 24 mm Hg lower at 100 mg.
options.B: Doubling the dose again to 200 mg would lower SBP by 48 mm Hg.
options.C: The 50 mg dose produced no reduction in SBP compared with placebo.
options.D: The placebo group had a lower mean SBP than either Hypertensol group.

explanation: Correct: A) Placebo 150, 50 mg 138 and 100 mg 126 mm Hg give differences from placebo of 12 and 24 mm Hg, so the difference grew with dose. Why the others are wrong: B) 200 mg was not tested, so extrapolating to 48 mm Hg is not supported. C) the 50 mg group was 12 mm Hg below placebo. D) placebo had the highest mean SBP (150), not the lowest.
trap: Extrapolating the observed dose trend beyond the tested doses.
